provenance: Deli Gallery, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Born in Barranquilla, Colombia, and raised in Miami to a Venezuelan mother and Egyptian father, Ilana Savdie draws from hybrid cultural inheritances to create paintings charged with transformation and resistance. Her vibrant compositions merge the theatrical language of the Carnaval de Barranquilla with a contemporary vocabulary of queerness, humor, and critique.  | | In Marimonda en reposo, Savdie revisits the Marimonda—a folkloric trickster central to the Barranquilla Carnival, known for mocking the social elite through parody and exaggeration. Traditionally a symbol of rebellion disguised as play, the Marimonda becomes in Savdie's hands a vehicle for examining power, gender, and performance. "The idea of the trickster as an agent of change and of humor as a mode of resistance," she notes, "is rooted in a really queer form of exaggerating the body." (Whitney Museum of American Art, "Minisode: Iiana Savdie and Carmen Maria Machado on trickery, horror, and the uncanny," October 2023, Audio Archive)  | | Savdie's material process mirrors this conceptual tension. Pouring and layering beeswax, oil, and acrylic, she cultivates contrasts between precision and accident—between the controlled line and the organic wrinkle. These corporeal surfaces evoke skin that leaks, folds, and transforms, rejecting ideals of perfection. The vivid palette of coral, teal, and magenta heightens the painting's dreamlike charge, where form seems to oscillate between figuration and abstraction.  | | Part of a pivotal series from 2020, Marimonda en reposo encapsulates Savdie's commitment to dismantling binaries—between grotesque and beautiful, discipline and desire. Both intimate and theatrical, the work affirms painting as a site of liberation: a place where pleasure, parody, and protest coexist in exuberant defiance.

material: etching, watercolor and gouache on paper
provenance: Carolina Nitsch Contemporary Art, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Executed in 2005, Black Arcs/Untitled (Black) belongs to the extraordinarily fertile final chapter of Louise Bourgeois's career, when she turned to drawing and printmaking as acts of meditation, introspection, and release. Working from her Chelsea townhouse studio until her passing in 2010, Bourgeois collaborated with Benjamin Shiff of the Osiris imprint to produce a series of complex, experimental works on paper that rearticulated her lifelong preoccupations including memory, trauma, motherhood, and the fragile balance between control and chaos. For an artist who once declared, "To create is an act of liberation and every day this need for liberation comes back to me," these late works reveal a distilled, essential form of self-expression. (P. Herkenhoff, Louise Bourgeois, Phaidon, 2003, p. 19)  | | In Black Arcs/Untitled (Black), Bourgeois employs etching, watercolor, and gouache to create an elegant rhythm of interlocking oval forms, rendered with both delicacy and tension. The repeated, almost pulsating patterns recall her Spiral series of the same period, where looping, vortex-like motifs symbolized psychological cycles of repression, rage, and renewal. The spiral was, for Bourgeois, a metaphor drawn from her childhood: she remembered watching workers twist and wring soaked tapestries in the River Bièvre near her family's restoration workshop — a gesture that embodied both care and violence. "The spiral is an attempt at controlling the chaos," she once said, "beginning at the outside is the fear of losing control; winding in is a retreating, a compacting to the point of disappearance." ('The Art of Louise Bourgeois', Tate, June 2016) In the present work, the curved lines verge on abstraction but retain an unmistakable corporeal charge, echoing the curving limbs and coiling forms of her monumental Spider sculptures — icons of maternity, resilience, and entrapment.  | | While Bourgeois is celebrated primarily for her large-scale sculptures, drawing was the medium through which her ideas were first conceived and continually reworked. As a child, she had filled in missing motifs on the tapestries her parents restored — an early act of image-making that marked the beginning of her artistic vocation and her lifelong dialogue between memory and creation. In the last decade of her life, she returned to these instincts with renewed urgency. Works such as Black Arcs/Untitled (Black) reveal the artist in full command of her expressive language in which she transforms fragility into structure, pain into rhythm, and the personal into the universal. The interlacing forms, hovering between tension and release, become visual metaphors for the endurance of the human psyche. Both intimate and monumental in feeling, the work embodies Bourgeois's lifelong negotiation between memory and healing and further stands as a testament to her enduring relevance as one of the most psychologically profound artists of the twentieth century.

King-Nero, eds., The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné: Paintings and Sculptures 1970-1974, Volume 3, New York, 2014, pl. 2749-2750, illustrated pp. 413-414. | | "Andy, in my mind, was fundamentally a voyeur. He had to go out and see and do and be seen to have the energy for his work." | - Robert Denison | | Robert J. Denison, a longtime friend and advisor to Andy Warhol, was first introduced to the art world by Dorothy and Roy Lichtenstein, his neighbors on Long Island. As chairman of the investment firm First Security Management, Denison counseled Warhol to establish the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts in Pittsburgh and was instrumental to the financial security of the Warhol legacy. In addition to advising Warhol, Denison also advised artists such as Roy Lichtenstein and Robert Rauschenberg, forever impacting the way artists capitalized on their artistic star power and secured their legacies. Warhol created these two silkscreen portraits, both of unique size, along with two additional portraits of his friend Denison, now held in the Andy Warhol Museum. Never before offered for sale, these two portraits have been in Denison's collection since their creation.   | | Denison's work in finance and advice to Warhol inspired both Warhol's 1980s  Dollar Sign and Gems series as well as his broader reflections on money. Warhol once remarked, "I'm convinced that if you can spell things out very simply and say everything clearly right away, you'll be a success in business. Like Bob Denison can do that." Denison's identity as a "money man" aligned perfectly with Warhol's portraiture practice from the early 1970s onward—one that critics have often discussed as reinventing the humanist genre through its engagement with the commodity form.  | | This pair of acrylic and silkscreen portraits of Denison belongs to Warhol's extensive series of society portraits begun in the 1970s, which defined the second half of his career. Warhol photographed his subjects using a Polaroid camera, transferring the instant print to an acetate to create a silkscreen stencil. Having started with photobooth reels in the 1960s, by the 1970s Warhol had adopted the Polaroid as his preferred tool. The transfer process allowed him to exercise artistic license—removing blemishes, altering hair color, and heightening contrast. Many portraits were commissions, and Warhol often chose color schemes that reflected the sitter's personality.  | | Drawing on his background as a 1950s commercial illustrator, Warhol skillfully employed mass-reproductive techniques and vivid color to command attention. The same strategies that informed his iconic portraits of Marilyn Monroe, Elvis Presley, and Elizabeth Taylor are evident in his society portrait series. Here, too, Bob Denison is distilled to his essence: cigarette in hand, his expression cool and detached. In a distinctly Warholian way, he performs his own identity.  | | At the time, curator Robert Rosenblum dubbed Warhol the "Court Painter of the '70s," likening his work in the portrait genre to John Singer Sargent and his late-nineteenth-century portrayals of the wealthy elite. Warhol's portraits, however, suited the "Me Generation," shaped by Watergate disillusionment and disco-era glamour. Sleeker and glossier than his 1960s celebrity silkscreens, these works echoed the polished aesthetics of Vogue and Vanity Fair. Among those immortalized alongside Denison were Debbie Harry, Liza Minnelli, and Gianni Versace. The Denison portraits, among the earlier examples in the series, feature the expressive, hand-painted acrylic details also found in Warhol's Chairman Mao works—a technique he had recently revived in the late 1960s and would abandon again by the end of the following decade.

Wiener, Walton Ford: Pancha Tantra, Cologne, 2015 (illustrated p. 175). | | | Born in 1960 and growing up in the Hudson Valley of New York, Walton Ford has always had a strong connection with the natural world. Ford graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1982 and soon established his reputation in traditional natural history illustration through his early depictions of indigenous birds throughout the 1990s. Ford expands on this tradition by incorporating a broader narrative often as commentary on the legacy of human impact to the environment.   | | The present work, El Poeta, completed in 2004, appears to be a continuation of his indigenous birds series which he began in the 1990s during a visit to India. The work depicts the Cuban Red Macaw, a now-extinct species of macaw that was native to Cuba and the Cuban Parrot. The central Macaw dominating the composition is ensnared in a trap while the Cuban Parrots below appeared to have walked into a baited snare. The inscriptions and title suggest a critique on the fate of the indigenous birds of North America whose demise is extrinsically linked to colonialism and western expansion.   | | Ford's work is included in a number of private and public collections, including the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville; the Detroit Institute of Arts, Detroit; the Minneapolis Institute of Art, Minneapolis; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Princeton University Art Museum, Princeton; the Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.; the Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford; and the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York amongst many others.

provenance: Estate of the artist. | Baumgartner Galleries, Inc., Washington, D.C. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | New York, The Museum of Modern Art, The Art of the Real: USA 1948-1968, July 3-September 8, 1968 (exh. cat., p.30, illustrated p. 31). | | Alphecca: the brightest star in the Corona Borealis and the jewel in its northern crown. Paul Feeley was an artist deeply attuned to the harmonies of cosmic order and the richness of Classical art and the age of Enlightenment. In the present work, we glimpse an almost hieroglyphic translation of a universal system. Rediscovered from long term ownership and presented at auction for the first time, Alphecca belongs to Feeley's celebrated series of 'jacks,' the radiant, cruciform compositions that are the signature of his mature style. Alphecca wonderfully embodies the austere resolve that enabled Feeley to produce some of the most visually arresting images of post-war abstraction. An artist, educator and curator who was deeply embedded in the Abstract Expressionist movement – famously Helen Frankenthaler's tutor at Bennington College, and collaborator with Clement Greenberg on multiple group exhibitions – his tragically curtailed career has left an enduring mark on twentieth century art history, holding an almost unique position as part of, but distinct from, Color Field and Hard-Edge painting. | | Across an unprimed canvas, five vivid red 'jacks' radiate in poised equilibrium, their rounded limbs echoing one another in a visual fugue of repetition and pause. Feeley's compositional rigor is underscored by his restraint: each form hand-drawn and rendered with calculated precision. The raw canvas ground creates an open field in which the geometry of Feeley's system operates, emphasizing the painting's architecture rather than its imagistic quality. The scarlet red 'jacks' of Alphecca sit firmly against the picture plane, giving an intense feeling of depth. It is a masterclass of abstract painting that deals as much with the phenomenological effects of technique as with the formal issues that weighed heavy on Abstract Expressionist and Minimalist practitioners. | | Included in the landmark exhibition The Art of the Real: USA 1948–1968 at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, Feeley's disciplined compositions stand apart from the declarative gestures of Abstract Expressionism and the impersonality of Minimalism. His work occupies a middle ground, intensely composed yet organic and tactile. Writing in the exhibition catalogue accompanying the 1968 show, E.C. Goossen notes that "the new attitude has been turning art inside out: instead of perceptual experience being accepted as the means to an end, it has become the end in itself. The Renaissance artist labored over perspective in order to create an illusion of space within which he could make believable the religious and philosophical ideals of his time; the contemporary artist labors to make art itself believable" (E.C. Goossen, The Art of the Real: USA 1948-1968, New York, 1968, p. 11). In this regard, we experience Feeley's 'jacks' literally as well as illusionistically. Like the star after which the present work is titled, there is a corollary relationship: we experience the real, enormous celestial bodies of our night sky as single flares of light amongst groups; our relationship to them is entirely abstract. Feeley's 'jacks' provide no more information to the spectator than their simple form amongst others, yet the magnitude of their presence lingers as a known unknown. | | Feeley's premature death in 1966 marked the loss of an artist of great sincerity and depth. Alphecca stands as proof of his quiet radicalism. His 'jacks' exemplify a vision of abstraction stripped of grandiosity yet charged with power and play. In its serene luminosity, Alphecca affirms Feeley's belief that painting could be both intellectual and corporeal; speak to cosmic order as readily as personal experience. The present work offers an opportunity to acquire one of the finest examples of Feeley's late works with exceptional period history, included in a seminal exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art that signaled the very best of post-war American painting.

Miami Herald, June 19, 2005, (illustrated p. 3M). | | Felix Gonzalez-Torress "Untitled" (1990) embodies a characteristic restraint and sensitivity, distilling profound emotional and conceptual resonance within the simplest of forms. Comprising a stack of pristine white sheets each embossed with a ring of dolphins, the work merges the visual language of Minimalism with intimate symbolism. The delicate circular impression—visible only when light grazes the surface—suggests continuity, motion, and infinity, while the dolphin introduces a gentle lyricism into the work's otherwise austere materiality.A recurring motif in his oeuvre, the dolphin holds layered symbolic weight within Gonzalez-Torres's visual lexicon. Often associated with intelligence, companionship, freedom and migration, it can be read as a metaphor for the artist's own life as an émigré from Cuba, navigating between cultures and identities. The circular formation of the animals evokes both the cyclical nature of return and the longing inherent in displacement—an emblem of community and exile, distance and reunion.Unlike his well-known participatory stacks, whose parameters allow viewers to choose to take sheets which can be replenished, "Untitled" complicates this interactive aspect of the work. Most other stack works are unique and can be manifested in more than one place at a time, and sheets can be endlessly replenished, however, "Untitled" is an editioned work whose sheets are finite and can never be replenished if they are taken, and as such, the owner may opt not to allow viewers to take from the work. By changing the stakes of physical engagement, the work may prompt questioning around generosity, value, and permanence.

provenance: Galeria Thomas Cohn, São Paulo. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Madrid, Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Guillermo Kuitca: Obras 1982/2002, 2003 (later traveled to Buenos Aires, Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires MALBA) (exh. cat., illustrated p. 122). | | Painted in 1988, L'Enfance du Christ stands as a haunting synthesis of Guillermo Kuitca's core themes: displacement, theater, architecture, and religion. Created during a pivotal period in the artist's career, the work transforms a domestic interior into a suspended, dreamlike stage. Rendered in rich gradations of red, black, and white, the scene unfolds like an aerial blueprint of a private home- its roof removed, walls exposed, and furniture frozen in quiet disarray.  | | The work's title references Hector Berlioz's 1854 oratorio L'Enfance du Christ, recounting the Holy Family's flight into Egypt. Kuitca reinterprets this sacred story through the lens of Argentina's post-dictatorship reality, embedding within it a meditation on exile, fear, and survival. The Holy Family's journey becomes an allegory for the artist's family history of migration and his generation, who came of age amid political violence and social dislocation. Born in Buenos Aires in 1961, Kuitca was a teenager during the years of military rule (1976–1983), a period marked by censorship, forced disappearances, and mass migration. The resulting sense of rupture and diaspora, both national and personal, pervades his imagery.  | | Visually, L'Enfance du Christ reveals Kuitca's fascination with the intersection between painting and theater. The composition recalls a theatrical set viewed from a bird's-eye perspective, an approach that denies architectural closure and complicates the viewer's position. By stripping away the roof and doors, Kuitca invites the viewer into an exposed, voyeuristic gaze, in turn granting access to a private world that is simultaneously abandoned and alive. The recurring absence of human figures heightens this tension: chairs, curtains, and a vase of flowers suggest human presence, yet their emptiness speaks to departure and loss.  | | The deep crimson tones that dominate the canvas convey a sense of corporeal intensity and emotional volatility. The light source emerging from the upper left corner imbues the scene with a theatrical glow, evoking both divine illumination and psychological unease. Kuitca's controlled palette reinforces the sensation of turbulence contained within silence, of history distilled into architectural form.  | | Religion and theatricality converge in this composition. After encountering Frida Kahlo's work in Madrid in the early 1980s, Kuitca began integrating Catholic and Latin American symbolism into his practice, despite his own Jewish upbringing. The sacred subject matter of L'Enfance du Christ thus marks an act of transgression and reconciliation—an attempt to bridge inherited faith and lived history through the visual language of theater.  | | Ultimately, L'Enfance du Christ embodies Kuitca's conviction that painting can serve as both mirror and stage for the human condition. It reflects the traumas of political exile, the fluidity of identity, and the enduring search for spiritual refuge. Through its haunting emptiness and architectural precision, the work offers not only a record of absence but also a profound meditation on the spaces where memory, belief, and loss intersect.
